power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Case line lists, which record dates of onset, recovery, and hospitalisation, are among the most granular data in infectious disease epidemiology and can provide insights into transmission dynamics.
Dynamic survival analysis (DSA) fits a deterministic, differential-equationbased model to line lists to estimate parameters such as infectivity and the infectious period.

Infectious periods are usually not exponential, and incorporating this into mechanistic models for line-list data often requires partial differential equation (PDE) schemes that can be difficult to implement and must be customised for each model, which may limit their use.
Here, we propose Discrete Dynamic Survival Analysis (DDSA), a discrete-time DSA for case line lists based on difference equations.

It matches calendar-day data directly without interpolation, and its log-likelihood is differentiable via forward-mode automatic differentiation, enabling off-the-shelf gradient-based samplers without model-specific numerical infrastructure.
Non-exponential infectious periods are accommodated through a boxcar model or a discrete analogue of the "device of stages".
We apply the DDSA method to three historical outbreaks of influenza A(H1N1), Ebola, and measles.

DDSA estimates of transmission parameters were close to published analyses where these were available, an agreement that partly reflects shared modelling choices, and the method handles incomplete line lists with missing onset or recovery dates.
Synthetic experiments show that recovery intervals identify the infectious period, while infection times and final size constrain R 0 when the population at risk is known.
Discrete DSA provides a simple, extensible framework for simulation and inference of infectious disease dynamics.

Mathematical models can offer insights into the transmission of infectious disease, allowing us to estimate key epidemiological quantities such as the reproductive number, forecast the number of new cases [1], and explore counterfactual scenarios, such as the impact of school closures or vaccination campaigns [2, 3].

text.text: Many models use aggregated case data i.e., counts of new cases per day or week, to infer model parameters.
However, deeper insights can be gained through the use of case line lists, which record individual-level event times such as symptom onset, hospitalisation, recovery, or death [4, 5].

text.text: While aggregate counts reveal general trends, line lists provide detailed tracking of individual events, allowing the estimation of key time dynamics, such as the infectious period.

In current practice, line-list data are analysed in several ways: direct survival analysis with parametric (e.g., exponential, lognormal or Weibull) natural-history interval models, which lack a mechanistic link to population-level transmission dynamics [6, 7].

KhudaBukhsh et al. [12] proposed a modelling paradigm, originally introduced as Survival Dynamical Systems (SDS) but now known as Dynamic Survival Analysis (DSA) [13] [14] [15], to fit dynamical models of disease transmission to line lists using concepts borrowed from survival analysis.

text.text: By assuming a large population size, DSA simplifies the analysis of line lists by using a mean-field model described by differential equations to compute the hazard of infection over time, and applying standard survival analysis techniques to estimate natural history parameters of infection.
This method has subsequently been extended to consider non-exponential distributions of key quantities such as the infectious period [13] and the impact of repeat testing in discrete time [16].

text.text: Variants of DSA have been used in multiple contexts, including Influenza A(H1N1) on a college campus [12], foot and mouth disease in the UK [13], Ebola in DRC [14, 17], and COVID-19 at a national level [13], at a state level [18, 19], in an individual prison [20], and on a college campus [16].

text.text: For simple models, such as the standard SIR, DSA involves solving a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to compute the hazard of infection, which can be obtained using standard numerical solvers [12].

text.text: The assumption of exponentially distributed infectious periods in these models is, however, often unrealistic.

Incorporating non-exponential distributions into DSA requires reformulating the transmission model using partial differential equations (PDEs) [13], which in turn typically require custom discretisation schemes.

text.text: Together, these requirements may limit the adoption of DSA in practice.
Most studies using DSA to date have employed a continuous time, differential equation based model to compute the infection hazard.

However, data such as symptom onset times and recovery times are normally recorded in the form of dates, thus continuous-time likelihoods must either interpolate the model's solution or treat observed dates as approximations to continuous event times.

Wascher et al. [16] avoided this in their interval DSA, which uses a discrete-time Reed-Frost-type SEIR model to estimate prevalence and time-varying transmission from repeated SARS-CoV-2 testing in a closed population.

text.text: Their model assumes a known population size and fixed sojourn-time distributions, and is fitted with a bespoke Metropolis-Hastings-within-Gibbs sampler that imputes individual infection and sojourn times.

More recently, Roy et al. [15] addressed this challenge for temporally aggregated count data by deriving a closed-form marginal likelihood that treats daily or weekly incidence as interval-censored observations in continuous time.

text.text: Here, we propose Discrete Dynamic Survival Analysis (DDSA), a discrete-time DSA for case line lists in which the population at risk can be either known or estimated, and extend it to non-geometric infectious period distributions and multiple groups, such as different age groups.
The primary aim of this study is to make DSA easier to apply to line lists recorded by date.

In discrete time, the likelihood is evaluated on the calendar days of the data, and such infectious periods are captured without potentially complex, model-specific numerical schemes, so that every model can be fitted with standard tools for Bayesian inference.
We implement the framework in Julia using Turing.jl [21], and demonstrate inference on simulated and real-world line list data.
text.formatted: We implement the framework in Julia using Turing.jl <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21]</ref>, and demonstrate inference on simulated and real-world line list data.

text.text: In DDSA, a recurrence map replaces the ODE and advances the epidemic state one step at a time, on the same time grid as the dated records.

No solver is needed, and the map is compatible with forward-mode automatic differentiation, allowing the application of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms such as the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) [22] directly.

text.text: In discrete time, infectious periods that are not exponential can be modelled using discrete phase-type (DPH) distributions, which are specified by finite sub-stochastic matrices [23].

text.text: They include the negative binomial and distributions with finite support, and can approximate others.
Their probability mass functions reduce to repeated matrix-vector products and are likewise differentiable with respect to the DPH parameters.
Time-varying parameters, for example a contact rate that changes after an intervention, can enter the map as one value per step (β k ), without changing how the likelihood is evaluated.

The result is a complete inference pipeline for line list data, including flexible dwell-time distributions and multi-group population structure, that can be expressed concisely in a standard probabilistic programming language without a custom numerical framework.

To meet this aim, we (i) derive the discrete-time DSA log-likelihood and show that it converges to the continuous-time formulation as ∆t → 0; (ii) extend it to non-geometric infectious periods through two representations, a boxcar (infection-age) model and a discrete analogue of the 'device of stages'; (iii) extend it to populations with multiple epidemiological groups; (iv) implement the full framework in Julia by fitting every model variant using the NUTS sampler in Turing.jl; and (v) assess what each part of the likelihood identifies, and how DDSA compares with continuous-time DSA, on synthetic data and on simulated outbreaks with known parameters.

We demonstrate DDSA through applications to line list data from three real outbreaks: influenza A(H1N1) at a university campus [12], Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo [14], and measles in Hagelloch, Germany, 1861 [24].

text.text: We accommodate such non-geometric infectious periods through two complementary discrete-time representations.
The Boxcar model tracks infection age and admits any discrete distribution through an age-specific hazard sequence.

The Generalized Linear Chain Trick (GLCT) instead chains staged compartments to approximate any distribution in the discrete phase-type family, needing more stages the less variable the distribution is.
Both change how the infected leave the infectious class in the map, and therefore τ and f , which modify the recovery term ℓ R of the likelihood.
Meanwhile, the form of the infection-time (ℓ I ) and final-size (ℓ constr ) components remain unchanged.
The two models use different DPHs.
The Boxcar model has one stage for each day of infection age, up to K age , where it is truncated.
This allows it to follow any hazard sequence, whether estimated from data or derived from a parametric distribution.
The GLCT map can represent any DPH, with one compartment per stage, and needs no truncation.
For the same infectious-period distribution, the two models produce the same susceptible trajectory, except for truncation at K age , which is negligible when P (W > K age ) is small.

The device-of-stages formulation may require fewer compartments than the boxcar model and avoids the need to truncate the infection-age distribution.

However, it requires committing to a specific parametric family: the number of stages r and their associated progression probabilities must be specified or inferred, rather than being determined directly from the data.
In contrast, the Boxcar representation accommodates any discrete distribution (empirical or parametric) simply by supplying the hazard sequence g a .
When a parametric family such as the negative binomial or Erlang is adopted, the two representations are equivalent and yield identical state trajectories for the same parameter values.

In such cases, the device-of-stages is preferred for its compact state vector and its compatibility with gradient-based samplers like NUTS, which benefit from the smooth, differentiable parameterisation of the phase-type transition matrix.

text.text: The analyses were implemented by evaluating the discrete recurrences from Section 2(b) directly within the likelihood, with continuous transition rates converted to per-step event probabilities via expressions of the form p = 1 -e -λ ∆t .
As a result, the log-posterior remains differentiable in the continuous parameters, allowing the use of gradient-based inference in Turing.jl.
Priors and bounds for every analysis are listed in Supplementary Section S1.
Integer-valued parameters had discrete uniform priors and were summed out of the likelihood.
Uniform priors were adopted in settings where epidemiologically motivated bounds could be specified from the data context.

For transmission and removal rates, upper bounds were chosen to exceed plausible values for the pathogen and population, while lower bounds preclude zero or near-zero rates that are inconsistent with an observed outbreak.
For initial infected fractions, a Beta prior concentrated near zero reflects the expectation of a small founding seed.
These uniform priors assign equal mass within their support and do not penalise values near the bounds, which can affect posterior shape when data are sparse.
Sensitivity to the prior bounds is examined in Supplementary Section S2.3.
However, log-normal or half-normal alternatives for rate parameters are a direction for future work.

All DDSA analyses used the same sampler settings: NUTS with four chains of 2,000 postwarm-up draws after 1,000 warm-up iterations, with 4,000 draws for the NegBin DPH and Boxcar fits of Scenario B. Chains were started from jittered data-based values, as chains started from prior draws occasionally became trapped in low-density regions in replicated simulations.
The convergence targets were R < 1.01 and ESS bulk ≥ 100 per parameter [40].

We therefore summed them out of the likelihood exactly over their finite support, under discrete uniform priors, so that every model was sampled with NUTS alone.

When a population size enters only the Binomial final-size term, the sum is a single pass over its support, with no further evaluations of the recurrence map.

When a parameter changes the map or the recovery distribution (the phase count r, or N 2 in the Hagelloch model, which also sets the seed ρ2 = 1/N 2 ), each value requires one evaluation of the map, and parameters that vary together are summed over their joint grid.
After sampling, the summed-out parameters were drawn, once per retained draw, from their exact conditional posterior, p(ψ | θ, D) ∝ π(ψ) e ℓ(θ,ψ).

text.text: The count model was fitted using four different configurations: an exponential infectious period with a Poisson likelihood, an exponential infectious period with a Negative-Binomial likelihood, a staged Erlang-4 infectious period with a Negative-Binomial likelihood, and an exponential infectious period with the removal rate fixed at 1/µ (where µ = 4 d is the mean of the continuous-time Erlang-4 infectious period from which the synthetic DPH is built).

The first three models estimated the removal rate jointly with the transmission rate.
In contrast, DDSA used the complete line list information, which included the infection day and recovery interval for each case, along with the final count of cases out of the 99 individuals at risk.

text.text: Adjusting one factor at a time (see Supplementary Section S2) showed that the loss of information on R 0 in the count models during this outbreak with a high attack rate (91 out of 99 infected individuals; the loss was smaller at moderate attack rates) can be attributed to a single likelihood term.

text.text: These durations had a mean of 7.95 days and a coefficient of variation of 0.22, below that of a geometric distribution with the same mean (0.94), so the infectious period was modelled with a Negative Binomial DPH.
Since every duration is at least δ min = 4 days, an offset Negative Binomial DPH was used.
This model consisted of δ min -r deterministic one-day stages followed by r geometric stages with progression probability p.
Its support starts at δ min , its mean is δ = δ min -r + r/p, and it requires that r ≤ δ min .
The model sampled δ and set p = r/(δ -δ min + r), so that δ keeps its meaning across values of r.
It was assumed that a single index case from Class 2 initiated the outbreak, so the initial infectious fraction was fixed at ρ = 1/N 2 for Class 2 and zero for Classes 0 and 1.

The line list partitions the population into three classes: pre-school children (Class 0, K0 = 90), younger school students (Class 1, K1 = 30), and older school students (Class 2, K2 = 68, including the index case).
Between-group transmission was captured using a 3×3 who-acquiresinfection-from-whom (WAIFW) matrix B, where B ij is the per-day transmission rate to group i from group j:
The per-step force of infection on group i is then 1 -exp(-Λ i ), where Λ i = ∑︁ j B ij I j and I j denotes the infectious fraction of group j.

Within-class transmission is governed by β C1 (Class 1) and β C2 (Class 2), a global term β G acts across all groups, and a school-topreschool term β H captures transmission from infectious school students to pre-school children.
This structure is a mean-field, group-level approximation of the individual-level contact model of Neal and Roberts [36] in its homogeneous-mixing form (their M θ model without distance decay).

text.text: The rates β C1 , β C2 and β G correspond to their classroom and global routes, and β H acts as a proxy for their same-household term.
In their model, the household term is applied between any two members of the same household.
However, as the compartmental model does not represent this, a single household rate was restricted to the school-to-preschool direction.

text.text: DDSA offers a method to estimate key epidemiological parameters, including the reproduction number, the distribution of the infectious period, and the effective size of the population at risk,   directly from line lists.

It reformulates the survival likelihood of dynamic survival analysis [12, 13] in discrete time, so that individual infection times, infectious-period durations and final size are evaluated on the calendar-day grid of the line list.
text.formatted: It reformulates the survival likelihood of dynamic survival analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13]</ref> in discrete time, so that individual infection times, infectious-period durations and final size are evaluated on the calendar-day grid of the line list.

text.text: DDSA has three practical advantages. (i) No continuous solution has to be interpolated onto observed dates. (ii) The infection-time PMF and the discrete phase-type recovery distribution are computed exactly by iterating the recurrence map.

As a result, a non-geometric infectious period requires neither a numerical PDE solve nor a numerical convolution. (iii) The likelihood can therefore be written directly in a standard probabilistic programming language and sampled with off-the-shelf NUTS, without model-specific numerical code.
Continuous-time DSA can also be sampled with NUTS, as our re-implementations were (Supplementary Section S3), but only with the addition of ODE and PDE solvers, which the discrete maps replace.
DDSA's estimates are comparable to those of continuous-time DSA.
On simulated outbreaks, the two methods agreed except when the daily step was coarse relative to epidemic growth (Supplementary Section S3; Limitations).
The continuous-time re-implementations used for this comparison were checked against the published codes [12, 13].

These roles also determine where a misspecified infectious period becomes visible.
Under a geometric infectious period, the incidence curves remained visually similar to those of the correctly specified DPH models.
Nevertheless, the estimates were biased in a direction set by the available data.
With the full line list, the recovery intervals held the mean infectious period near its true value, and R 0 was inflated by 14%.

With infection times only, the final size held R 0 near the value implied by the observed attack rate (posterior median 2.70, against 2.74 from the final-size relation; truth 3.16, inside the 95% CrI), while β was inflated by 60% and the mean infectious period was roughly halved.
Only the recovery intervals revealed the misspecification.

Comparing DDSA with count models separates what is lost by aggregating the data from what is lost by choosing a count likelihood.
In this high-attack-rate outbreak, Poisson and Negative-Binomial count models did not identify R 0 because they omit the individuals who were never infected, not because the data were aggregated.
With N known, a count model with a never-infected cell recovered the DDSA estimate of R 0 from infection times alone, without recovery intervals and without fixing the removal rate.
At lower attack rates, a Poisson count model also constrained R 0 , although less precisely (Supplementary Section S2), so this loss should not be generalised to all incidence-only analyses.

Without the never-infected count, R 0 was constrained closely only once the removal rate was fixed, consistent with KhudaBukhsh et al. [12] and Putter et al. [45], who also fixed the recovery-time distribution because only incidence was observed.

The two approaches are complementary.
Countbased DSA needs only incidence data, which are more widely available, whereas line lists add individual recovery intervals, which identify the infectious period directly.

Where data collection can be planned, these results suggest recording, in addition to onset dates, the date each case stops being infectious (or a removal proxy such as hospitalisation) and the size of the population at risk.
Surveillance line lists are rarely complete.
In the analyses considered here, the DDSA likelihood served as the core observation model.
It was supplemented with survivor terms for right-censored recoveries in the H1N1 case study, and with a convolution over latent onset times for hospitalisation-only Ebola records.

The Hagelloch case study was used to stress-test DDSA on a heterogeneous, group-structured outbreak, where school-centred and within-household transmission depart from homogeneous mixing.
The three-group model needed only a 3 × 3 transmission matrix in the same recurrence map.
It reproduced the qualitative finding of the individual-level analysis of Neal and Roberts [36], with more transmission within classroom 1 than within classroom 2 (P (β C1 > β C2 ) = 0.996).

text.text: The GLCT and Boxcar implementations gave closely matching summaries (R0 = 2.17), an internal check that the two discrete representations agree when the dwell-time family is shared.
The stress test also exposed the limits of the mean-field approximation in this setting.
The model underpredicted the attack rates of Classes 0 and 2, brought the class epidemics closer together in time than observed, and placed N 0 and N 2 near their upper bounds.
The stage cap was also binding (Section 3(e)).
More generally, other compartmental structures can be accommodated within DDSA provided the mean-field basis of the survival likelihood is preserved.

Additional compartments and further stratification into demographic groups or spatial patches, for example, all follow from the same difference-equation construction, as the Hagelloch model illustrates.
These structures assume a closed population in which each individual is infected at most once.
As a result, the susceptible population S k only decreases, and the final-size term applies.
Extending DDSA to endemic transmission, with births, waning immunity or reinfection, would require changes to the map and to the likelihood.
The map would need inflows to the susceptible class and initial conditions near the endemic state rather than a small seed.
Additionally, since S k would no longer only decrease, the infection-time distribution would be constructed based on the per-step incidence S k h k rather than relying on the differences in S k .
In this context, individual survival would be defined by the hazard h k from the moment a person becomes susceptible.
Furthermore, the final-size term would be replaced by a term representing the number of cases within the observation window, reflecting the person-time at risk.
The only term that may remain unchanged would be the recovery-interval term.
These extensions were not implemented here and are left for future work.
The case studies highlight limitations of data fidelity and observational proxies.
Not all event times used in the case studies were independently observed.

In the H1N1 dataset, recovery times were generated using an exponential infectious period with a mean of 5.5 d, so that case study is best interpreted as a demonstration of the discrete inference framework under inherited assumptions, and the estimate of γ as a consistency check.
It was retained as it provides a direct comparison with the survival-analytic approach of KhudaBukhsh et al. [12].

text.text: Additionally, in the Ebola analyses, hospitalisation was used as a proxy for removal.

The inferred infectious period should therefore be read as a model-based removal interval tied to the observation process, and the R 0 values are conditional on that definition and on the observation window.
For the same reason, the population sizes N , N w and N 0 -N 2 are best read as effective at-risk sizes within the chosen model and window, not as total population sizes.
The recording of a case is part of the same observation process.

Cases missed at a constant rate are absorbed into these effective sizes (Section 2(c)(ii)), although in Hagelloch, where the class sizes were bounded, missed cases would also have lowered the estimated R 0 .

However, if recording practices changed during an outbreak, for example as case finding improved, or if they depended on the duration or severity of a person's illness, this would affect the infection-time curve or the recorded infectious periods.
Such changes were not modelled here, and would be hard to separate from changes in transmission using the line list alone.
The transmission models rely on simplifying assumptions that DDSA shares with continuoustime DSA.
Mean-field forces of infection average over individual-level heterogeneity in contacts, which can be a poor match when transmission is concentrated in households or classrooms.
In Hagelloch, for example, the group-level model underpredicted the attack rates of Classes 0 and 2 by about 15% and brought the class epidemics closer together in time than observed.
The analyses also assume a closed population over the observation window, which suits single outbreaks but not endemic transmission.
The same assumptions affect how uncertainty is represented.
The predictive bands reflect only parameter uncertainty, so they do not include day-to-day variation, which a chain-binomial version of the GLCT or Boxcar map would add.
In addition, the infection-time likelihood treats infections as independent draws from the meanfield curve.
In simulated epidemics, intervals for the infectious period, informed by individual recovery intervals, were generally close to nominal.
Credible intervals for R 0 were narrower than nominal even with the correct model.

Nominal 95% intervals covered the true R 0 in 17-80% of outbreaks, least often near R0 = 1, whereas coverage was close to nominal on data drawn independently from the mean-field curve (Supplementary Section S4).
The R 0 intervals of the Ebola waves, whose R 0 is close to 1, may therefore understate the uncertainty.
Methods that may correct the R 0 intervals are outside the scope of this study.
The discrete-time formulation also carries a predictable step-size dependence.
At ∆t = 1 d the DPH means exceed the corresponding continuous-time Erlang means, so estimates must be converted before they are compared with continuous-time ones.
In simulations, the daily step also affected estimates in two ways (Supplementary Section S4.2).
When continuous-time infectious periods were recorded by day, same-day removals became one-day intervals, which biased the mean infectious period upward by about 2%.
When the epidemic grew quickly, R 0 was biased upward.
At R0 = 4, DDSA estimates exceeded those of continuous-time DSA by 7-9% by the end of the outbreak.
A finer time step removed the first bias and reduced the second.
The GLCT map, built stage by stage, allows at most one stage transition per day, so r cannot exceed the shortest recorded interval, and a single short interval can set this limit.
In simulations, this cap overstated the variability of the infectious period and biased R 0 upward (Supplementary Section S4.3).
The Boxcar map accepts a law without this minimum and so has no such cap, although its R 0 intervals remained narrower than nominal at the daily step.

Coxian or branched DPHs (Section 2(b)(ii)), in which an early exit or a branch with few stages can take the short intervals, may relax the cap and allow a less variable infectious period, but fitting them was left for future work.
Each analysis uses a single ∆t, so data recorded at different reporting intervals would need to be aggregated or entered as interval-censored terms.
As the present case studies use uniform daily cadences, neither adjustment was necessary.
Finally, on the computational side, all DDSA analyses in the main text used one set of sampler settings (Section 2(d)), which met the convergence targets here but has not been tested more widely.
Summing integer-valued parameters out of the likelihood is exact, but its cost grows with the summed support whenever the parameter changes the recurrence map.
For instance, the Hagelloch model evaluates the map for each of the 40 combinations of r and N 2 at every gradient, which makes it the most computationally demanding analysis.
Other automatic-differentiation backends may perform differently, but these were not tested.
We have presented Discrete Dynamic Survival Analysis (DDSA), a discrete-time reformulation of dynamic survival analysis for calendar-day epidemic line lists.

The DDSA likelihood has the same three components as continuous-time DSA (infection times, recovery intervals and final size), but each is a discrete analogue computed from a difference-equation map that replaces the continuous-time ODE.
Infection times enter through a Multinomial distribution over calendar days, recovery intervals through discrete phase-type distributions, and the final size through a Binomial term.

These components converge to their continuous-time counterparts as ∆t → 0, and each is computed exactly by iterating the map, without solver-based interpolation or custom numerical schemes for non-geometric infectious periods.
They are differentiable in the continuous parameters, so gradient-based inference runs in standard probabilistic programming frameworks without model-specific numerical code.

Applied to three historical outbreaks of influenza, Ebola, and measles, under both homogeneous and group-structured compartmental models, DDSA accommodated incomplete line lists through composable likelihood terms for right-censored recoveries and missing onset times.
Where published continuous-time DSA analyses were available (influenza and Ebola), its estimates were similar, except for the effective population size and reproduction number for H1N1.
This agreement partly reflects shared modelling choices.
Synthetic experiments showed that each type of data plays a different inferential role.
Infection times determine the growth rate, the number never infected bounds R 0 when the population at risk is known, and recovery intervals identify the infectious period.
As a result, a misspecified infectious-period shape biased the estimates while leaving the incidence fit visibly unchanged.
Only the recovery intervals revealed it.
When recovery intervals were observed, the misspecification inflated the estimated reproduction number.
Without them, it inflated the transmission rate and shortened the infectious period.

By keeping discrete-time inference aligned with the calendar-day structure of line-list data while remaining expressible in standard probabilistic programming tools, DDSA offers a transparent and extensible route to fitting mean-field epidemic models of single outbreaks to individual-level records.
